all-of-switzerland.text: By late July a brown-yellow belt stretched across much of Switzerland, above all the Mittelland and the Jura, where last year’s meadows and fields have visibly dried out. The 2026 image is from 24 July, when two cloud-free orbits covered the country; a narrow strip in the west lies between them. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
all-of-switzerland.title: All of Switzerland

baselland.text: Satellite images from the end of May and the beginning of July 2026. Sissach lies in the centre, Liestal in the far north-west. Within six weeks much of the green farmland in the Ergolz valley and its side valleys turned brown.
baselland.title: Baselland

forests-near-brugg-ag.text: The forests around Brugg look brown and thinned. Beech, the second most common tree in Switzerland, is hit hardest: the leaves of exposed trees have turned yellow, orange and brown, and some trees have already dropped them. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
forests-near-brugg-ag.title: Forests near Brugg AG

great-aletsch-glacier.text: From the slopes of Bettmeralp and Fiescheralp to the glacier itself, the comparison shows one of the most striking changes. After another winter with little snow, early summer heat removed the protective snow cover from the glacier by the end of June, much earlier than usual. Dark, bare ice now covers a far larger area instead of bright old snow. (Source: watson.ch)
great-aletsch-glacier.title: Great Aletsch Glacier

gurbetal-and-aare-valley.text: Brown instead of green on fields and meadows: before and after the June heat. In many places June brought only 20–50 % of the normal rainfall, with temperatures about 3 °C above the long-term average. The view south of Bern shows the Gürbetal, the Belpberg and the Aare valley at Münsingen, the area of the SRF image. (Source: SRF Meteo, 9 July 2026)
gurbetal-and-aare-valley.title: Gürbetal and Aare valley

interlaken-be.text: In the Bernese Oberland the drought is much less visible than in the Mittelland, partly because strong glacier melt keeps streams and rivers high and local storms brought moisture. South-facing slopes still show drier meadows and thinner forests. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
interlaken-be.title: Interlaken BE

konstanz-and-untersee.text: The water level of the Untersee is the lowest of the 1991–2020 reference period. Wide, pale strips of exposed shore appear where water normally stands; boat jetties were already lying on dry ground in April. 8 August 2025 compared with the same day in 2026. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
konstanz-and-untersee.title: Konstanz and Untersee

lake-constance-untersee.text: Persistent drought has pushed the Untersee to a historic low. Around the island of Werd, wide gravel banks lie dry. At 25 centimetres below the previous record, the water level in August is lower than at any time since at least 1930. 8 August 2025 compared with the same day in 2026. (Source: Blick, 12 August 2026)
lake-constance-untersee.title: Lake Constance – Untersee

lake-lucerne.text: Less brown than other regions: local thunderstorms brought some relief, and the wooded slopes of the Rigi and Pilatus stay green in places. Many meadows and fields have nevertheless dried out. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
lake-lucerne.title: Lake Lucerne

lakes-neuchatel-and-murten.text: One of Switzerland’s main vegetable-growing areas: lighter and brown patches show between the plots of the Three Lakes Region, and the foot of the Jura is among the areas with the largest soil-moisture deficit. Watson compares 8 August; the nearest clear swissEO image of 2026 here is from 11 August. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
lakes-neuchatel-and-murten.title: Lakes Neuchâtel and Murten

upper-lake-zurich.text: Very little rain fell here in the preceding weeks; thunderstorms visible on the radar often brought little or nothing. The result is dried-out meadows and brown fields around the upper lake. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
upper-lake-zurich.title: Upper Lake Zurich

wil-sg-and-surroundings.text: The hilly landscape of streams and pastures around Wil is clearly browner than a year ago. Small streams react quickly to a lack of rain because, unlike large lakes, they have no buffer. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
wil-sg-and-surroundings.title: Wil SG and surroundings

zurich-airport.text: Where lush green fields surrounded the airport a year ago, brown and beige now dominate this intensively farmed area. The change is most visible on the unirrigated meadows next to the runways. (Source: watson.ch, 10 August 2026)
zurich-airport.title: Zurich Airport

agri.description:
# Agriculture composite

This composite uses short-wave infrared, near-infrared and blue bands to monitor crop health (a band is a region of the electromagnetic spectrum; a satellite sensor can image Earth in different bands). Both short-wave and near infrared bands are particularly good at highlighting dense vegetation, which appears dark green in the composite. Crops appear in a vibrant green and bare earth appears magenta.



More info [here](https://eo.belspo.be/en/colour-composites) and [here.](https://gisgeography.com/sentinel-2-bands-combinations/)
agri.name: Agriculture
agri.subtitle: Based on bands B11, B08, B02

analyst.description:
# NDVI difference to a reference date

Method of the NDVI Analyst by Raffael Bienz (Canton of Aargau): the NDVI difference between two dates (later minus earlier), using swissEO S2-SR reflectance with negative values set to 0, masked to forest. Changes are pixels with an NDVI drop below the threshold (default −0.08); a 3 × 3 majority filter removes edge effects. *Detected change* shows the binary result. The statistics of an area of interest report the forest area and the affected area in ha and %, with and without edge-effect removal, like the original script.

More info [here](https://github.com/RaffiBienz/ndvi_analyst).
analyst.name: NDVI difference to a reference date
analyst.subtitle: NDVI change between two dates in forest, with change detection

barren.description:
# Barren Soil Visualization

The Barren Soil Visualization can be useful for soil mapping, to investigate the location of landslides or the extent of erosion in non-vegetated areas. This visualization shows all vegetation in green and the barren ground in red. Water appears black.



More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/barren_soil/) and [here.](https://medium.com/sentinel-hub/create-useful-and-beautiful-satellite-images-with-custom-scripts-8ef0e6a474c6)
barren.name: Barren Soil
barren.subtitle: Based on the combination: BSI, B08, B11

evi.description:
# Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI)

The enhanced vegetation index (EVI) is an 'optimized' vegetation index as it corrects for soil background signals and atmospheric influences. It is very useful in areas of dense canopy cover. The range of values for EVI is -1 to 1, with healthy vegetation generally around 0.20 to 0.80.





More infos [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/evi/) and [here.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_vegetation_index)
evi.name: EVI
evi.subtitle: Enhanced Vegetation Index

fdc.description:
# Forest Disturbance Classification

A LightGBM classification of forest disturbances by Jonas Viehweger and Martin Puhm (Joanneum Research, EvoLand project), published as a Sentinel Hub custom script. From a single date it assigns every pixel to *bark beetle* (brown), *clear cut* (grey), *salvage logged* (grey too, low confidence), *wildfire* (dark brown) or *windthrow* (blue); *healthy* forest is not drawn. It was trained on samples from Germany, Sweden and Spain (macro F1 0.83), works best on recent, large disturbances and is only valid on forest, so the forest mask is on by default. Expect classification errors and validate the results.

**Input scaling:** the trees split on Sentinel Hub L2A digital numbers in the convention DN = 10000 × reflectance (data before processing baseline 04.00, e.g. the script's 2019 example). swissEO stores DN = (ρ + 0.1) × 10000, so the script receives DN − 1000, clamped at 0. The Copernicus Browser feeds recent scenes without removing the offset (see the README on harmonizeValues), so its result can differ there. The 150 trees are loaded unchanged from the script on first use.

More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/forest_disturbance_classification/).
fdc.name: Forest Disturbance Classification
fdc.subtitle: Bark beetle, clear cut, wildfire, windthrow (Sentinel Hub custom script)

geo.description:
# Geology 12, 8, 2 composite

This composite uses short-wave infrared (SWIR) band 12 to differentiate among different rock types (a band is a region of the electromagnetic spectrum; a satellite sensor can image Earth in different bands). Each rock and mineral type reflects short-wave infrared light differently, making it possible to map out geology by comparing reflected SWIR light. Near infrared (NIR) band 8 highlights vegetation and band 2 detects moisture, both contributing to differentiation of ground materials. The composite is useful for finding geological formations and features (e.g. faults, fractures), lithology (e.g. granite, basalt, etc.) and mining applications.



More info [here.](https://www.euspaceimaging.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/EUSI-SWIR.pdf)
geo.name: Geology 12, 8, 2
geo.subtitle: Based on bands B12, B8, B2

hon.description:
# Highlight Optimized Natural Color

This script aims to display the Earth in beautiful natural color images. It uses highlight optimization to avoid burnt out pixels and to even out the exposure.



More info [here.](https://sentinel-hub.github.io/custom-scripts/sentinel-2/highlight_optimized_natural_color/#)
hon.name: Highlight Optimized Natural Color
hon.subtitle: Enhanced natural color visualisation

mstress.description:
# NDMI for Moisture Stress

The Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI) for moisture stress can be used to detect irrigation. For all the index values above 0, knowing the land use and land cover, it is possible to determine whether irrigation has taken place. Knowing the type of crop grown (e.g. citrus crops), it is possible to identify whether irrigation is being effective or not during the crucial growing summer season, as well as find out if some parts of the farm are being under or over-irrigated.





More info [here.](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/ndmi_special/#)
mstress.name: Moisture Stress
mstress.subtitle: Classified NDMI for irrigation

nbr.description:
# Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR)

Normalized Burn Ratio is frequently used to estimate burn severity. It uses near-infrared (NIR) and shortwave-infrared (SWIR) wavelengths. Healthy vegetation has a high reflectance in the near-infrared portion of the spectrum, and a low short-wave infrared reflectance. On the other hand, burned areas have a high shortwave infrared reflectance but low reflectance in the near infrared Darker pixels indicate burned areas.



More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/custom-scripts/sentinel-2/nbr/).
nbr.name: Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR)
nbr.subtitle: Based on a combination of bands (B8 - B12)/(B8 + B12)

nddi.description:
# Normalized Difference Drought Index (NDDI)

The NDDI (Gu et al. 2007) combines vegetation greenness (NDVI) and vegetation water content (NDWI): NDDI = (NDVI − NDWI) / (NDVI + NDWI). Vegetation under drought stress has less water and less green, which raises the NDDI (red). By default the NDWI is computed from NIR and SWIR (B08, B11), as in the original paper; values are clipped to −1…1.

The openEO drought notebook uses the Awesome Spectral Indices formula with an NDWI from green and NIR (B03, B08), selectable as *Green*. With it NDVI + NDWI is close to zero over vegetation, and almost every pixel ends up at −1 or +1 (99.8 % in a test over Aarau, independent of the reflectance offset), so the map is saturated.

More info [here](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006GL029127) and in the [openEO notebook](https://github.com/Open-EO/openeo-community-examples/blob/main/python/50_thematic-notebooks/drought-nddi/drought-nddi.ipynb).
nddi.name: NDDI
nddi.subtitle: Normalized Difference Drought Index (Gu et al. 2007)

nddichg.description:
# NDDI change vs. previous year

Difference between the NDDI of the selected date and the NDDI one year earlier, as in the openEO drought notebook, which compares a drought year with a baseline year. Positive values (red) mean drier conditions than a year ago, negative values (blue) wetter. The NDWI is computed from NIR and SWIR (Gu et al. 2007) by default; the notebook's green NDWI is selectable but saturates. The reference uses the acquisitions within ±20 days of the same day one year earlier (or of a reference date you choose), clearest first; each pixel takes the first one with clear data. Unlike the notebook, which averages May–July, single dates are compared, so clouds and cloud shadows are masked on both sides by default.

More info [here](https://github.com/Open-EO/openeo-community-examples/blob/main/python/50_thematic-notebooks/drought-nddi/drought-nddi.ipynb).
nddichg.name: NDDI change vs. previous year
nddichg.subtitle: NDDI of the date minus NDDI one year earlier

ndmi.description:
# Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI)

The normalized difference moisture Index (NDMI) is used to determine vegetation water content and monitor droughts. The value range of the NDMI is -1 to 1. Negative values of NDMI (values approaching -1) correspond to barren soil. Values around zero (-0.2 to 0.4) generally correspond to water stress. High, positive values represent high canopy without water stress (approximately 0.4 to 1).



More info [here.](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/ndmi/)
ndmi.name: Moisture index
ndmi.subtitle: Based on a combination of bands (B8A - B11)/(B8A + B11)

ndsi.description:
# Normalised Difference Snow Index (NDSI)

The Sentinel-2 normalised difference snow index can be used to differentiate between cloud and snow cover as snow absorbs in the short-wave infrared light, but reflects the visible light, whereas cloud is generally reflective in both wavelengths. Snow cover is represented in bright vivid blue.



More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/ndsi/).
ndsi.name: NDSI
ndsi.subtitle: Based on a combination of bands (B3 - B11)/(B3 + B11)

ndvi.description:
# Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)

The normalized difference vegetation index is a simple, but effective index for quantifying green vegetation. It is a measure of the state of vegetation health based on how plants reflect light at certain wavelengths. The value range of the NDVI is -1 to 1. Negative values of NDVI (values approaching -1) correspond to water. Values close to zero (-0.1to 0.1) generally correspond to barren areas of rock, sand, or snow. Low, positive values represent shrub and grassland (approximately 0.2 to 0.4), while high values indicate temperate and tropical rainforests (values approaching 1).

More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/ndvi/).
ndvi.name: NDVI
ndvi.subtitle: Based on a combination of bands (B8 - B4)/(B8 + B4)

ndvidiff.description:
# swissEO NDVIdiff

The NDVI changes show the difference between the vegetation's state of the current year compared to the previous year as observed by satellites, for the forest areas of Switzerland at 10 m. Negative values (red) mean less vital vegetation than a year ago, positive values (green) more. The product is published for the end of July, August and September; the product nearest to the selected date is shown. Grey: missing data.

More info [here](https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/en/satelliteimage-swisseo-ndvidiff) and in the [content information](https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/dam/en/sd-web/bODfHY8ioFyS/swissEO_NDVIdiff_AdditionalContentInfo.pdf).
ndvidiff.name: swissEO NDVIdiff
ndvidiff.subtitle: NDVI change: current vs. previous year (forest)

ndvidiff2.description:
# swissEO NDVIdiff v200 BETA

**Beta version, not an official product.** Year-on-year NDVI change for the forest areas of Switzerland at 10 m, computed from **cloud-free two-month mosaics** of swissEO S2-SR v200 instead of single acquisitions. Three overlapping windows per year: June/July, July/August and August/September, each named after its end date (31 July, 31 August, 30 September); the window nearest to the selected date is shown.

**Mosaic** ([main_cloudfree_mosaic_csde.py](https://github.com/swisstopo/topo-satromo-v2/blob/dev-20261006/main_functions/main_cloudfree_mosaic_csde.py)): for every pixel and band (B02, B03, B04, B08) all observations of the window are used; observations flagged by the cloud mask (1, 2, 3), outside the scene footprint or in terrain shadow (200) are discarded, and the **first quartile** of the remaining values is taken, following the Sentinel-2 quarterly mosaic algorithm of the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem, more robust to cloud and haze residues than the first cloud-free value or the mean.

**NDVI difference** ([test_reprocess_ndvidiff_csde.py](https://github.com/swisstopo/topo-satromo-v2/blob/dev-20261006/main_functions/test_reprocess_ndvidiff_csde.py)): NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red) from the reflectance of the mosaic (ρ = DN × 0.0001 − 0.1), minus the NDVI of the same window one year earlier; Int16, value / 1000, no data 32701. Negative values (red) mean less vital vegetation than a year ago, positive values (green) more.

The COGs are published as examples on cms.geo.admin.ch, not in the STAC catalogue.
ndvidiff2.name: swissEO NDVIdiff v200 BETA
ndvidiff2.subtitle: BETA: NDVI change of two-month cloud-free mosaics vs. the previous year (forest)

ndviz.description:
# swissEO NDVIz

The NDVI anomalies show the current vegetation vitality as observed by satellites, as a z-score relative to the long-term behaviour, for the forest areas of Switzerland at 10 m. Negative values (brown) mean lower vitality than usual, positive values (green) higher. The product is published for the end of July, August and September; the product nearest to the selected date is shown. Grey: missing data.

More info [here](https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/en/satelliteimage-swisseo-ndviz) and in the [content information](https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/dam/en/sd-web/mZTj7kABmTrD/swissEO_NDVIz_AdditionalContentInfo.pdf).
ndviz.name: swissEO NDVIz
ndviz.subtitle: NDVI anomaly as z-score (forest)

ndwi.description:
# Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI)

The normalized difference water index is most appropriate for water body mapping. Values of water bodies are larger than 0.5. Vegetation has smaller values. Built-up features have positive values between zero and 0.2.



More info [here.](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/ndwi/)
ndwi.name: NDWI
ndwi.subtitle: Based on a combination of bands (B3 - B8)/(B3 + B8)

nir.description:
# False color composite

A false color composite uses at least one non-visible wavelength to image Earth. The false color composite using near infrared, red and green bands is very popular (a band is a region of the electromagnetic spectrum; a satellite sensor can image Earth in different bands). The false colour composite is most commonly used to assess plant density and health, since plants reflect near infrared and green light, while they absorb red. Cities and exposed ground are grey or tan, and water appears blue or black.



More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/false_color_infrared/) and [here.](https://eo.belspo.be/en/colour-composites)
nir.name: False color
nir.subtitle: Based on bands B8, B4, B3

savi.description:
# Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index (SAVI)

 The Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index is similar to Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) but is used in areas where vegetative cover is low (< 40%). The index is a transformation technique that minimizes soil brightness influences from spectral vegetation indices involving red and near-infrared (NIR) wavelengths. The index is helpful when analysing young crops, arid regions with sparse vegetation and exposed soil surfaces.





More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/savi/) and [here.](https://eos.com/blog/6-spectral-indexes-on-top-of-ndvi-to-make-your-vegetation-analysis-complete/)
savi.name: SAVI
savi.subtitle: Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index

scl.description:
# Scene classification



Scene classification was developed to distinguish between cloudy pixels, clear pixels and water pixels of Sentinel-2 data and is a result of ESA's Scene classification algorithm. Twelve different classifications are provided including classes of clouds, vegetation, soils/desert, water and snow. It does not constitute a land cover classification map in a strict sense.



More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/scene-classification/).
scl.name: Scene classification map
scl.subtitle: Classification of Sentinel-2 data as result of ESA's Scene classification algorithm.

swir.description:
# Short wave infrared composite (SWIR)

Short wave infrared (SWIR) measurements can help scientists estimate how much water is present in plants and soil, as water absorbs SWIR wavelengths. Short wave infrared bands (a band is a region of the electromagnetic spectrum; a satellite sensor can image Earth in different bands) are also useful for distinguishing between cloud types (water clouds versus ice clouds), snow and ice, all of which appear white in visible light. In this composite vegetation appears in shades of green, soils and built-up areas are in various shades of brown, and water appears black. Newly burned land reflects strongly in SWIR bands, making them valuable for mapping fire damages. Each rock type reflects shortwave infrared light differently, making it possible to map out geology by comparing reflected SWIR light.



More info [here.](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/swir-rgb/)
swir.name: SWIR
swir.subtitle: Based on bands B12, B8A, B4

terrain.description: Solar incidence angle 0–180° from sun azimuth and zenith, plus shadow (value 200: cast or self-shadow) from swissSURFACE3D at acquisition time.
terrain.name: Terrain / solar incidence
terrain.subtitle: Based on the terrain mask band

true.description:
# True color (TCI)

The true color image delivered with each swissEO S2-SR mosaic (asset `tci_10m`): the visible bands red (B04), green (B03) and blue (B02) rendered as an 8-bit RGB image at 10 m, representing the Earth as humans would naturally see it. It is shown as delivered; gain, gamma and the RGB ranges can be adjusted on top, and the cloud, shadow and vegetation masks apply. Statistics and the pixel inspector use the reflectance bands.

More info [here](https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/en/satelliteimage-swisseo-s2-sr).
true.name: True color
true.subtitle: TCI, based on bands B4, B3, B2

urban.description:
# False Color Urban composite

This composite is used to visualise urbanized areas more clearly. Vegetation is visible in shades of green, while urbanized areas are represented by white, grey, or purple. Soils, sand, and minerals are shown in a variety of colors. Snow and ice appear as dark blue, and water as black or blue. Flooded areas are very dark blue and almost black. The composite is useful for detecting wildfires and calderas of volcanoes, as they are displayed in shades of red and yellow.



More info [here](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/sentinel-2/false-color-urban-rgb/) and [here.](https://eos.com/false-color/)
urban.name: False color (urban)
urban.subtitle: Based on bands B12, B11, B4

vhi.description: Map of forest condition based on the VHI (Vegetation Health Index), which reflects the current state of forest in relation to historical data 1991-2020. The index is based on satellite data (Meteosat, Landsat 5,7,8, and Sentinel-2) of different spatial resolutions, aggregated of ten and thirty metres respectively. The VHI consists of two components: one part (VCI - Vegetation Condition Index) represents the local biophysical conditions of the vegetation, and the other part (TCI - Thermal Condition Index) characterizes the climatic conditions (temperature). Both components depict the current situation in relation to a reference period. The combined VHI is used to assess drought and other disturbances or stress factors; the lower the value, the greater the stress and its impact on vegetation. Values from 100 down to 60 indicate excellent vegetation condition, values up to 50 are good, and values up to 40 are normal. Below 40, the vegetation shows signs of stress, up to 30 it is lightly stressed, up to 20 stressed, up to 10 severely stressed and values below 10 indicate an extremely stressed vegetation condition. The forest area is shown on the map, providing a robust indicator of the regional vegetation conditions. The dataset was developed in collaboration with MeteoSwiss for the federal drought portal. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data.
vhi.name: swissEO VHI forest
vhi.subtitle: Vegetation Health Index over forest, vs. 1991–2020

vhidef.description:
# VHI cumulative deficit

The cumulative forest health deficit of the [Waldtrockenheit dashboard](https://waldtrockenheit-dashboard.vercel.app/vhi.html), computed **per pixel** instead of per warning region. For every day from 1 April to the selected day (at most 31 October), the daily swissEO VHI forest map contributes 40 − VHI where the VHI is below 40, the threshold for *stressed*; a VHI of 40 or more adds nothing. A very low VHI therefore raises the sum strongly, and the sum can only grow during the season.

Only days with a VHI value count. In long periods without satellite images the VHI is missing once its 7-day window has passed, so those days add nothing and the deficit can be underestimated; the pixel inspector and the statistics show the number of days with data. Only pixels inside the VHI forest mask count (non-forest stays transparent). The dashboard rates each region against its 2018 to 2025 climatology; per pixel this would need eight seasons of daily maps, so the colours use a fixed scale here (adjustable).

The sums are computed in the browser from the daily COGs (about 30 per month), so the first view of a season takes a while; the sums are kept for the session, and stepping forward through the dates (or a timelapse) only reads the days in between.

More info [here](https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/en/satelliteimage-swisseo-vhi).
vhidef.name: VHI cumulative deficit
vhidef.subtitle: Cumulative forest health deficit Σ(40 − VHI) since 1 April (forest)

vhiext.description:
# VHI days in extreme stress

The number of days in extreme stress of the [Waldtrockenheit dashboard](https://waldtrockenheit-dashboard.vercel.app/vhi.html), computed **per pixel**: the days from 1 April to the selected day (at most 31 October) on which the daily swissEO VHI forest map is below 10 (*extremely stressed*). As in the dashboard the days are counted in total, not consecutively, because a counter of consecutive days would reset at every short cool or wet spell without the forest actually recovering. Classes as in the dashboard: 0, 1 to 5, 6 to 15, 16 to 30 and more than 30 days.

Days without a VHI value do not count (see *VHI cumulative deficit*).

More info [here](https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/en/satelliteimage-swisseo-vhi).
vhiext.name: VHI days in extreme stress
vhiext.subtitle: Number of days with VHI below 10 since 1 April (forest)

vhiveg.description: Map of vegetation condition based on the VHI (Vegetation Health Index), which reflects the current state of vegetation in relation to historical data 1991-2020. The index is based on satellite data (Meteosat, Landsat 5,7,8, and Sentinel-2) of different spatial resolutions, aggregated to ten and thirty metres respectively. The VHI consists of two components: one part (VCI - Vegetation Condition Index) represents the local biophysical conditions of the vegetation, and the other part (TCI - Thermal Condition Index) characterizes the climatic conditions (temperature). Both components depict the current situation in relation to a reference period. The combined VHI is used to assess drought and other disturbances or stress factors; the lower the value, the greater the stress and its impact on vegetation. Values from 100 down to 60 indicate excellent vegetation condition, values up to 50 are good, and values up to 40 are normal. Below 40, the vegetation shows signs of stress, up to 30 it is lightly stressed, up to 20 stressed, up to 10 severely stressed and values below 10 indicate an extremely stressed vegetation condition. The entire vegetation area is shown on the map view to provide a complete overview of the regional vegetation status. The dataset was developed in collaboration with MeteoSwiss for the federal drought portal. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data.
vhiveg.name: swissEO VHI vegetation
vhiveg.subtitle: Vegetation Health Index over all vegetation, vs. 1991–2020
